extracted.intended_audience: advanced undergraduate or graduate students of mathematical logic / recursion theory; readers learning undecidability, Gödel's theorem, and recursive function theory
extracted.subtask_description: A textbook exposition of decidability, representability, Gödel/Tarski/Church theorems, the arithmetical hierarchy, and the theory of recursive (and recursively enumerable) functions and partial functions, with definitions, lemmas, and proofs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed-point Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: Given any formula β in which only v1 occurs free, we can find a sentence σ such that AE ! [σ ↔ β(S(σ)0)]. (Informally: there is a sentence σ that indirectly says “β is true of me.”)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof via a formula θ(v1,v2,v3) that functionally represents the coding function; construct a formula (1) ∀v3[θ(v1,v1,v3) → β(v3)], let q be its Gödel number, and replace v1 by S q 0 to obtain σ. The lemma is used to produce self-referential sentences (used in Tarski and Gödel proofs).

rubrics_metrics.name: Tarski Undefinability Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: Th N (the set of true sentences of N) is not definable in N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply the fixed-point lemma to ¬β to construct σ with |=N [σ ↔ ¬β(S(σ)0)]; this yields a sentence that shows any candidate β defining Th N fails (it would produce a liar-style contradiction). Immediate corollary: Th N is not recursive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary: Th N not recursive
rubrics_metrics.description: The set Th N is not recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any recursive set is definable in N (Corollary 34B); since Th N is not definable by Tarski, it cannot be recursive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gödel Incompleteness Theorem (1931)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A ⊆ Th N and (A) (the set of Gödel numbers of A) is recursive, then Cn A is not a complete theory. Thus there is no complete recursive axiomatization of Th N.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof: If Cn A were complete then Cn A = Th N, but Th N is not recursive while a complete recursively axiomatizable theory would have recursive set of consequences (item 21, Sec. 3.4). Also view via fixed-point sentence σ that is true but not provable from A.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 35B (adding an axiom preserves recursiveness of consequences)
rubrics_metrics.description: If (Cn A) is recursive then (Cn(A; τ)) is recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalence: α ∈ Cn(A; τ) ⇔ (τ → α) ∈ Cn A. Therefore membership reduces to checking whether a constructed sentence is in Cn A; recursiveness follows from previous results about recognizing Gödel-coded constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 35C (Strong undecidability of Cn AE)
rubrics_metrics.description: Let T be a theory such that T ∪ AE is consistent. Then (T) is not recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assume (T) recursive; since AE finite, apply Lemma 35B to get (Cn(T ∪ AE)) recursive. Use fixed-point lemma to get σ with AE ! [σ ↔ ¬β(S(σ)0)] where β represents (T). Diagonal argument leads to contradiction with consistency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 35D (no complete recursive axiomatization)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is recursive and A ∪ AE is consistent, then Cn A is not complete.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A complete recursively axiomatizable theory would be recursive (item 21, Sec. 3.4), contradicting Theorem 35C which shows (Cn A) is not recursive.

rubrics_metrics.name: Church's Theorem (1936)
rubrics_metrics.description: The set of Gödel numbers of valid sentences (in the language of N) is not recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Special case of strong undecidability: take T to be the theory of all valid sentences. The result generalizes to languages with at least a two-place predicate symbol; some very limited languages (equality-only) can have decidable validities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: recursively enumerable (r.e.) relation
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation R on N is recursively enumerable iff R = {a | ∃b (a,b) ∈ Q} for some recursive Q. Equivalently, R is the domain of some recursive relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Standard abbreviation r.e.; also called computably enumerable (c.e.) when using 'computable' instead of 'recursive'. Recursively enumerable relations are definable in N by existential formulas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 35E (equivalent characterizations of r.e.)
rubrics_metrics.description: For an m-ary relation R, the following are equivalent: (1) R is r.e.; (2) R is the domain of some recursive relation Q; (3) R = {a | ∃b (a,b) ∈ Q} for some recursive (m+1)-ary Q; (4) same with finitely many existential quantifiers over a recursive (m+n)-ary Q.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof shows how multiple existential quantifiers can be collapsed into a single one via encoding sequences; establishes r.e. = domains of recursive relations and the usual Σ1 form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 35F (recursive iff both it and complement r.e.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation is recursive iff it and its complement are both recursively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If recursive, both are r.e. Conversely, given r.e. enumerations for P and its complement, define f(a) = least b showing membership in either enumeration; f is recursive and decides P by checking which enumeration witnessed membership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 35G (effective enumerability characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation is effectively enumerable iff it is the domain of a decidable relation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Q is effectively enumerated by a procedure, then 'a appears within n steps' is decidable and has domain Q. Conversely, to enumerate domain of decidable R, dovetail checks over m and output matching tuples when found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corollary 35H (Church's thesis, second form)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation is effectively enumerable iff it is recursively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identifies effective procedures with recursive functions/relations; the two forms of Church's thesis are equivalent via Theorem 35F and Theorem 17F.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 35I (Cn A is r.e. when axioms are recursive)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a set of sentences with (A) recursive, then (Cn A) is recursively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Matches the informal fact that a theory with decidable axioms is effectively enumerable: enumerate deductions and output their conclusions; but Cn A need not be recursive (Theorem 35C).

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: weak representability in a theory T
rubrics_metrics.description: A formula ψ(v1,...,vn) weakly represents an n-ary relation Q in theory T iff for every a1,...,an in N, (a1,...,an) ∈ Q ⇔ ψ(Sa1 0,...,San 0) ∈ T.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is 'half' of representability: for members of Q the theory proves the instance; for nonmembers the theory may not prove the negation unless Q is recursive. ω-consistency considerations apply when deriving equivalences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 35J (weak representability iff r.e.)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation is weakly representable in Cn AE iff it is recursively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If Q r.e., write Q = ∃b R(a,b) with recursive R and represent R in Cn AE to produce ψ; conversely, if ψ weakly represents Q, then membership reduces to existence of a deduction of ψ(Sa...), hence is r.e. via coding deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Arithmetical Hierarchy (Σk / Πk classes)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define Σ1 as the class of r.e. relations, Π1 as their complements; Σk consists of relations of the form ∃b1 ∀b2 ··· Q(a,b1,...,bk) with Q recursive (quantifier alternation beginning with ∃), and Πk similarly with quantifier alternation beginning with ∀.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equivalently, Σk relations are domains of Πk−1 relations; Σ0 (or Δ0) are recursive relations. Many techniques (collapsing existential blocks into one quantified sequence) are used to place relations in levels. Theorem 35K: arithmetical relations = ⋃k Σk = ⋃l Πl.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 35K (arithmetical relations characterization)
rubrics_metrics.description: A relation on N is arithmetical (definable in N) iff it is in Σk for some k, equivalently in Πl for some l.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every arithmetical relation has a prenex form; quantifier-free part defines a recursive relation, so the relation lies at some finite level of the hierarchy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 35L (closure of Cn under arithmetical class)
rubrics_metrics.description: If A is a set of sentences with (A) in Σk (k > 0), then (Cn A) is also in Σk.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof reduces membership in Cn A to a definable property about sequences of formula codes and uses the Σk description of (A) to push the classification through the construction of deductions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of Tm (Kleene normal form machinery)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each m, Tm is the (m+2)-ary relation: (e,a1,...,am,k) ∈ Tm iff (i) e is Gödel number of formula ϕ with free vars v1..vm,vm+1; (ii) k is sequence of length 2 and (k)0 is G of a deduction from AE of ϕ(Sa1 0,...,Sam 0, S((k)1)0).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Intended as coding of 'e is a program and k encodes a deduction witnessing that the output (k)1 is f(a1,...,am)'. Lemma 36A: each Tm is recursive. U(k) = (k)1 is the upshot function (recursive).

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma 36A (Tm is recursive)
rubrics_metrics.description: For each m, the relation Tm is recursive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Membership in Tm can be checked by verifying syntactic conditions: e codes a formula, k a suitable sequence encoding a deduction; previous coding results yield recursiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 36B (Kleene Normal Form / Universal machine)
rubrics_metrics.description: (a) For any recursive function f : Nm → N, there is an e such that for all a1,...,am, f(a1,...,am) = U(μk (e,a1,...,am,k) ∈ Tm). (b) Conversely, any e with ∀a ∃k (e,a,k) ∈ Tm defines a recursive function via the same normal form.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpretation: there is a universal recursive relation Tm and upshot U so that running 'program code' e on input a enumerates k witnesses; the least such k yields the output. This justifies a stored-program universal computer for recursive functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Theorem 36C (computable partial functions ↔ r.e. relations)
rubrics_metrics.description: An m-place partial function f is computable iff f (as an (m+1)-ary relation) is effectively enumerable (i.e., r.e.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If f computable, enumerate its graph by dovetailing computations on inputs; conversely if graph r.e. enumerate tuples and output values when pairs appear. Total computable functions correspond to decidable graphs; partial ones need not.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition: recursive partial function
rubrics_metrics.description: A recursive partial function is a partial function whose graph (as an (m+1)-ary relation) is recursively enumerable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the precise counterpart to 'computable partial function' when identifying effective procedures with recursive relations (Church's thesis). Examples: characteristic function of nonrecursive set is nonrecursive; many standard functions are recursive.
